topics.title: Communication: Concepts and Definition
topics.definition: Communication is the process of exchanging information, ideas and feelings between two or more people so that meaning is shared.

children.title: Definition and elements
children.definition: Sender, message, encoding, channel, receiver, decoding, feedback and noise make up the communication process.

children.title: Importance of communication
children.definition: It coordinates work, builds relationships, supports decision making and prevents misunderstanding.

children.title: Objectives of communication
children.definition: To inform, persuade, instruct, motivate, warn, educate and build goodwill.

card.explanation: Communication is the exchange of information, ideas and feelings so that meaning is shared. The process has eight parts: a sender who has an idea, a message, the encoding of it, a channel, a receiver, decoding, feedback and noise. It matters because work cannot be coordinated without it, and most workplace problems trace back to a message that did not land. The objectives vary: to inform, to persuade, to instruct, to motivate, to warn, to educate and to build goodwill. A message written without knowing which objective it serves usually serves none.
card.example: A notice saying the lab will be closed on Friday informs. The same notice explaining why, and asking for patience, builds goodwill as well.

quiz.q: How many elements does the communication process have?
quiz.why: Sender, message, encoding, channel, receiver, decoding, feedback and noise make eight.

quiz.q: What is the channel in the communication process?
options: The idea in the sender's head
The medium the message travels along
quiz.why: The channel is the path, whether spoken words, a letter, email or a telephone line.

quiz.q: Which statement about communication is NOT correct?
options: Decoding is the receiver turning the message back into meaning
Feedback confirms that the message was understood
Noise helps the message travel faster
Encoding turns an idea into a message
quiz.why: Noise is anything that distorts the message, so it always works against understanding.

quiz.q: Which objective is served by a safety warning notice?
quiz.why: A warning aims to change behaviour by making a risk known, which is the warn objective.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT listed as an objective of communication?
quiz.why: The objectives are to inform, persuade, instruct, motivate, warn, educate and build goodwill.

card.examTip: Name the eight elements in order, then list the seven objectives with one example each.

topics.title: Process and Models of Communication
topics.definition: Models simplify the communication process and show where meanings can be lost.

children.title: Shannon and Weaver model
children.definition: A linear model with source, encoder, channel, decoder, destination and noise.

children.title: Berlo SMCR model
children.definition: Source, message, channel and receiver, each influenced by skills, attitudes and knowledge.

children.title: Transactional and interactive models
children.definition: Communication is a simultaneous two way exchange in which both parties send and receive at once.

children.title: Feedback and noise in the process
children.definition: Feedback confirms understanding while noise - physical, semantic or psychological - distorts the message.

card.explanation: Models are simplified pictures of communication that show where meaning can be lost. The Shannon and Weaver model is linear. A source encodes a message, it travels through a channel, and a decoder receives it at the destination. Noise may enter anywhere along the way. Berlo's SMCR model names source, message, channel and receiver, and adds that each is affected by skills, attitudes and knowledge. Neither model shows a reply, so interactive and transactional models were added. In a transactional view both people send and receive at the same time.
card.example: A lecturer explaining a topic is the Shannon and Weaver chain. The students' puzzled faces are feedback, which the linear model leaves out and the transactional model includes.

quiz.q: Which model is linear and includes noise?
quiz.why: Shannon and Weaver drew the chain from source to destination with noise anywhere in between.

quiz.q: What does SMCR stand for in Berlo's model?
quiz.why: The four parts are Source, Message, Channel and Receiver, each shaped by skills and attitudes.

quiz.q: Which statement about models is NOT correct?
options: Linear models do not show feedback
Noise can enter at any point in the channel
A transactional model has both parties sending and receiving
Berlo's model ignores the people and studies only the channel
quiz.why: Berlo's model is the one that examines the people, through skills, attitudes and knowledge.

quiz.q: What type of noise is caused by a word having two meanings?
quiz.why: Semantic noise comes from the meaning of words, while physical noise is sound and psychological noise is bias.

quiz.q: Which model treats communication as simultaneous rather than one way?
quiz.why: In a transactional view both parties are senders and receivers at the same moment.

card.examTip: Draw the Shannon and Weaver chain, label where noise enters, then list SMCR and what shapes each part.

topics.title: Types and Modes of Communication
topics.definition: Communication is classified by the medium used and the direction of flow.

children.title: Verbal and non verbal communication
children.definition: Words carry the content while tone, gestures and expressions carry much of the meaning.

children.title: Oral and written communication
children.definition: Oral is fast and personal with immediate feedback; written is permanent, precise and easier to audit.

children.title: Formal and informal communication
children.definition: Formal follows the official chain of command while informal flows through the grapevine.

children.title: Interpersonal and intrapersonal communication
children.definition: Interpersonal is between two or more people while intrapersonal is the internal conversation within oneself.

children.title: One way and two way communication
children.definition: Two way communication includes feedback and therefore reduces misunderstanding.

card.explanation: Communication is grouped by the medium and by the direction the message travels. Verbal communication uses words, while non verbal uses tone, gestures, expression and posture, and the two must agree. Oral communication is fast and gives immediate feedback, while written communication is permanent, precise and easy to check later. Formal communication follows the official chain of command, and the informal grapevine runs alongside it. Interpersonal communication happens between people, and intrapersonal is the conversation you have with yourself before you speak.
card.example: A circular from the principal is formal and written. Two students discussing it in the corridor afterwards is informal and oral, and it usually travels faster.

quiz.q: Which type of communication is permanent and easy to check later?
quiz.why: A written record can be reread and produced as evidence, which is why contracts are written.

quiz.q: What is the informal channel of communication called?
quiz.why: The grapevine carries unofficial news quickly, and it exists in every organisation.

quiz.q: Which statement about types is NOT correct?
options: One way communication is always more accurate than two way
Non verbal signals include tone and posture
Intrapersonal communication happens within one person
quiz.why: Two way communication allows feedback, and that is what reduces misunderstanding.

quiz.q: Communication between two or more people is called:
quiz.why: Inter means between people, while intra means within one person.

quiz.q: Why must verbal and non verbal messages agree?
options: Because the receiver trusts the non verbal signal when the two clash
quiz.why: When the two disagree, people believe the body language, and credibility is lost.

card.examTip: List the five pairs of types and give one workplace example of each.

topics.title: Barriers to Communication and the Commandments of Communication
topics.definition: Barriers are obstacles that distort or block a message, and the commandments are the basic rules that prevent them.

children.title: Physical and environmental barriers
children.definition: Noise, distance, poor network connection and uncomfortable surroundings.

children.title: Semantic and language barriers
children.definition: Jargon, poor vocabulary, bad grammar and words with several meanings.

children.title: Psychological and emotional barriers
children.definition: Prejudice, fear, lack of attention, stress and distrust.

children.title: Organisational and cultural barriers
children.definition: Long chains of command, information overload, status differences and cultural differences.

children.title: Commandments of good communication
children.definition: Be clear, concise, complete, correct, courteous, concrete and considerate - the seven C principles.

card.explanation: Barriers are anything that distorts or blocks a message. Physical barriers are noise, distance, a poor network connection or an uncomfortable room. Semantic barriers come from jargon, a thin vocabulary, bad grammar and words with more than one meaning. Psychological barriers include prejudice, fear, stress, distrust and plain inattention. Organisational and cultural barriers are long chains of command, information overload, status gaps and cultural difference. The antidote is the seven C principles: clear, concise, complete, correct, courteous, concrete and considerate.
card.example: A message full of technical jargon sent to a non technical client hits a semantic barrier. Rewriting it in plain words removes the barrier at once.

quiz.q: Which barrier is caused by jargon and words with several meanings?
quiz.why: Semantic barriers arise from the meaning of the words, not from the channel used.

quiz.q: How many C principles are there in good communication?
quiz.why: The seven are clear, concise, complete, correct, courteous, concrete and considerate.

quiz.q: Which statement about barriers is NOT correct?
options: A long chain of command is an organisational barrier
Information overload improves the accuracy of a message
Noise and distance are physical barriers
Prejudice and stress are psychological barriers
quiz.why: Too much information is a barrier, because the receiver stops attending to any of it.

quiz.q: Which principle is followed when a message avoids unnecessary words?
quiz.why: Conciseness means saying what is needed in as few words as possible.

quiz.q: A receiver distrusts the sender and ignores the message. What kind of barrier is this?
quiz.why: Distrust is an emotional or psychological barrier, and clarity alone will not remove it.

card.examTip: Name the four barrier groups with two examples each, then write the seven C principles in full.

modules.title: Developing Communication Skills: Reading, Writing, Listening and Speaking

topics.title: Reading Skills
topics.definition: Reading is the active skill of deriving meaning from written symbols, and it can be made faster and more purposeful.

children.title: Preparation before reading
children.definition: Define the purpose, skim the layout, and decide what information is needed.

children.title: Reading styles
children.definition: Skimming for the gist, scanning for a specific fact, intensive reading for detail and extensive reading for pleasure.

children.title: Linear and faster reading
children.definition: Linear reading follows the text from start to finish while faster reading uses eye movement control and avoids sub-vocalisation.

children.title: Reading techniques
children.definition: SQ3R - survey, question, read, recite and review - along with note making, underlining and summarising.

card.explanation: Reading is an active skill, not a passive one, and it can be made faster with practice. Before starting, decide the purpose and what information you actually need, then skim the layout to see where things are. Four styles cover most needs: skimming for the gist, scanning for one fact, intensive reading for full detail and extensive reading for pleasure. Faster reading depends on controlling eye movement and dropping the habit of saying words silently to yourself. The SQ3R method ties it together: survey, question, read, recite and review.
card.example: Looking for one date in a textbook is scanning. Reading a whole chapter to answer an exam question is intensive reading, and SQ3R suits it best.

quiz.q: What does SQ3R stand for?
quiz.why: The five steps are survey, question, read, recite and review, in that order.

quiz.q: Which reading style is used to find one specific fact quickly?
quiz.why: Scanning moves the eye down the page looking for a known word or number.

quiz.q: Which statement about reading is NOT correct?
options: Skimming gives the gist of a passage
Intensive reading is for full detail
Deciding the purpose first saves time
quiz.why: Saying words silently holds reading to speaking speed, which is why faster reading drops the habit.

quiz.q: What is the first step of SQ3R?
quiz.why: Survey means looking over the headings, introduction and summary before reading properly.

quiz.q: Reading a novel for enjoyment is an example of:
quiz.why: Extensive reading covers long texts for pleasure and general understanding.

card.examTip: Name the four reading styles with a use for each, then write out the five SQ3R steps.

topics.title: Writing Skills
topics.definition: Effective writing is clear, correct and organised for a known reader and a defined purpose.

children.title: Principles of effective writing
children.definition: Clarity, brevity, accuracy, coherence and appropriate tone, with a logical introduction, body and conclusion.

children.title: Report writing
children.definition: Formal documents with title, terms of reference, procedure, findings, conclusions and recommendations.

children.title: Speech writing
children.definition: Written to be heard, with a strong opening, signposted body and memorable conclusion.

children.title: Minutes and agenda writing
children.definition: The agenda lists items to be discussed and the minutes record decisions, attendance and action points.

children.title: Letters and correspondence
children.definition: Formal letters follow a fixed layout with sender address, date, receiver address, subject, salutation, body and closing.

children.title: Article writing
children.definition: Explains or argues a point for a general reader with a headline, introduction, main points and conclusion.

children.title: Improving English language writing
children.definition: Build vocabulary, revise grammar, read good writing and edit ruthlessly.

children.title: When to write and when not to write
children.definition: Write when a record, precision or evidence is needed; speak when urgency or discussion is needed.

card.explanation: Effective writing is clear, correct and organised for a reader you have in mind. The principles are clarity, brevity, accuracy, coherence and a tone that suits the reader, arranged as an introduction, a body and a conclusion. Different documents have fixed shapes: a report carries terms of reference, procedure, findings, conclusions and recommendations. A speech is written to be heard, so it needs a strong opening and a memorable close. Minutes record decisions and action points, while the agenda lists what will be discussed beforehand.
card.example: An email that buries the request in the fourth paragraph fails on coherence. Putting the request in the first line and the reason after it usually gets a faster reply.

quiz.q: Which section of a report states what the report was asked to examine?
quiz.why: The terms of reference fix the scope, which is why they come near the beginning.

quiz.q: What is the difference between an agenda and minutes?
options: Minutes are used only in courts
The agenda is written after, the minutes before
The agenda lists what will be discussed, the minutes record what was decided
quiz.why: The agenda goes out before the meeting, and the minutes are the record taken during it.

quiz.q: Which statement about writing is NOT correct?
options: A speech is written to be heard, not read
A formal letter follows a fixed layout
The body of a document should raise points in random order
quiz.why: Coherence means the points are ordered so the reader can follow the argument.

quiz.q: When should you choose speaking over writing?
options: When urgency or discussion is needed
When a permanent record is needed
quiz.why: Discussion resolves things faster, while writing suits records, precision and evidence.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the principles listed for effective writing?
quiz.why: Length is not a principle on its own; brevity covers saying what is needed in few words.

card.examTip: Give the layout of a formal report in order, then a formal letter, and state when to speak rather than write.

topics.title: Listening Skills
topics.definition: Listening is the conscious effort to hear and understand a message, and it is the most used communication skill.

children.title: Importance and advantages of listening
children.definition: Good listening builds trust, reduces errors, improves decisions and saves the time lost in repeated work.

children.title: Art of listening
children.definition: Attention, patience, eye contact, avoiding interruption and reflecting the meaning back.

children.title: Types of listening
children.definition: Active, passive, empathetic, critical, appreciative and discriminative listening.

children.title: Barriers to listening and listening tests
children.definition: Distraction, premature evaluation, boredom and bias; listening tests use passages followed by questions to measure comprehension.

card.explanation: Listening is the conscious effort to hear and understand, and it is the communication skill people use most. Good listening builds trust, cuts errors, improves decisions and saves the time lost in doing work twice. The art of it is attention, patience, eye contact, not interrupting, and reflecting the meaning back in your own words. Types include active, passive, empathetic, critical, appreciative and discriminative listening. The common barriers are distraction, judging too early, boredom and bias, and listening tests measure comprehension with a passage followed by questions.
card.example: In a listening test the passage is played once, so noting key words as you hear them is what makes the questions answerable afterwards.

quiz.q: Which type of listening aims to understand the speaker's feelings?
quiz.why: Empathetic listening puts the listener in the speaker's position, which is what builds trust.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a barrier to listening?
quiz.why: Eye contact is part of good listening, while the other three block it.

quiz.q: Which statement about listening is NOT correct?
options: It is the most used communication skill
Reflecting the meaning back confirms understanding
quiz.why: Interrupting breaks the speaker's thread and signals that the reply matters more than the message.

quiz.q: What does a listening test usually measure?
options: Comprehension of a passage through questions
quiz.why: The test plays or reads a passage and then asks questions to check what was understood.

quiz.q: Judging a speaker's point before they finish is which barrier?
quiz.why: Forming a verdict early stops the rest of the message being heard at all.

card.examTip: List the six types of listening, then give the four barriers and five habits of good listening.

topics.title: Speaking Skills
topics.definition: Speaking is the process of conveying ideas orally with clarity, confidence and suitable tone.

children.title: Art of conversation
children.definition: Starting, maintaining and closing a conversation, taking turns, showing interest and avoiding argument.

children.title: Telephone and telephonic etiquette
children.definition: Identify yourself, speak clearly, keep it brief, listen actively and close politely.

children.title: Methods of asking questions
children.definition: Open, closed, leading, probing and rhetorical questions achieve different purposes.

children.title: Brainstorming and presenting reports
children.definition: Generate many ideas without judgement first, then organise and present the chosen ones with evidence.

children.title: Improving speech delivery
children.definition: Pace, pause, pitch, volume, pronunciation and the avoidance of filler words.

children.title: Expressing techniques
children.definition: Choosing the right words and tone, using examples and being concise.

card.explanation: Speaking conveys ideas orally with clarity, confidence and a tone that suits the occasion. Conversation has a shape of its own: an opening, turns that are shared, and a close, with interest shown throughout. On the telephone, identify yourself, speak clearly, keep it brief and close politely, because the other person has only your voice to go by. Questions do different jobs: open questions invite detail, closed ones confirm a fact, and probing ones go deeper. Delivery improves when pace, pause, pitch, volume and pronunciation are controlled.
card.example: Asking did you finish the report gets a yes. Asking where the report got to opens a conversation and usually tells you more.

quiz.q: Which type of question invites a detailed answer?
quiz.why: Open questions begin with what, how or why, which asks the other person to explain.

quiz.q: Which statement about speaking is NOT correct?
options: Reading a script word for word is the best delivery
Voice pitch and pace should vary
quiz.why: Reading aloud loses eye contact and sounds flat, which is why notes and outlines are preferred.

quiz.q: Why is telephone etiquette stricter than face to face conversation?
options: The listener has only the voice, with no gestures to help
quiz.why: Without facial expression and posture, clarity and tone carry the whole message.

quiz.q: What is the first rule of brainstorming?
options: Let the most senior person speak first
Judge each idea as it comes
Generate many ideas without judging them first
quiz.why: Judgement stops the flow, so ideas are collected first and evaluated afterwards.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT part of speech delivery?
quiz.why: Pace, pause, pitch, volume and pronunciation shape delivery, while handwriting belongs to writing.

card.examTip: Give the five parts of delivery, the question types, and three rules of telephone etiquette.

topics.title: Interview Techniques
topics.definition: An interview is a planned conversation in which an employer and a candidate assess each other.

children.title: What an interview is and why it matters
children.definition: It verifies the application, checks communication and attitude, and gives the employer evidence beyond the resume.

children.title: Types of interviews
children.definition: Structured, unstructured, semi structured, panel, group, stress, telephonic, video and walk in interviews.

children.title: Understanding the intricacies
children.definition: Interviewers look for knowledge, clarity of thought, attitude and cultural fit as well as qualifications.

children.title: Planning for an interview
children.definition: Research the organisation and role, prepare examples with STAR - situation, task, action and result - and plan logistics.

children.title: Answering skills
children.definition: Listen fully, answer to the point, structure with examples and never bluff.

children.title: Effective communication during interviews
children.definition: Dress appropriately, keep good posture and eye contact, speak at a measured pace and thank the panel.

children.title: TIPS to remember
children.definition: Think before answering, be honest, present yourself confidently and stay positive about past employers.

children.title: Mock interview
children.definition: A practice session that builds confidence and exposes weak answers before the real thing.

card.explanation: An interview is a planned conversation in which the employer and the candidate assess each other. It matters because it checks what a resume cannot: how you think, how you speak and how you react under pressure. Types include structured, unstructured, panel, group, stress, telephonic, video and walk in interviews. Preparation is research: learn what the organisation does and what the role needs. Have examples ready using the STAR shape: situation, task, action and result. During the interview, listen to the whole question, answer to the point, and never bluff.
card.example: Asked to describe a difficulty you solved, answer with the situation, the task you were given, the action you took and the result. A story with those four parts is easy to follow and easy to remember.

quiz.q: What does STAR stand for when preparing interview answers?
quiz.why: The four parts keep an example short and complete instead of rambling.

quiz.q: Which interview type uses a fixed set of questions for every candidate?
quiz.why: A structured interview asks everyone the same questions, which makes comparison fairer.

quiz.q: Which statement about interviews is NOT correct?
options: Posture and eye contact are part of the impression
Research the organisation before you go
Bluffing is better than admitting a gap
Listen to the whole question before answering
quiz.why: A bluff is usually exposed by one follow up question, and it costs more than an honest answer.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a mock interview?
options: To practise answers and expose weak ones before the real thing
quiz.why: Practice builds confidence and shows which answers still need work.

quiz.q: Which interview type deliberately puts the candidate under pressure?
quiz.why: A stress interview tests composure with sharp or unexpected questions.

card.examTip: List five interview types, then give the four STAR parts and three rules for answering.

topics.title: Group Discussion
topics.definition: A group discussion is a purposeful conversation among several candidates evaluated for content, communication and teamwork.

children.title: Purpose of group discussion
children.definition: To assess knowledge, reasoning, leadership, listening and the ability to work in a team.

children.title: Process and getting started
children.definition: Introduction of the topic, individual opinions, agreement building and conclusion within a time limit.

children.title: Preparation
children.definition: Read widely, keep facts and statistics ready and practise speaking in groups.

children.title: Art of guiding and controlling discussion
children.definition: Enter early and politely, keep the group on track and manage dominant speakers.

children.title: Personality test through group discussion
children.definition: Evaluators observe initiative, cooperation, patience and clarity under pressure.

children.title: Lateral thinking
children.definition: Looking at the same problem from an unexpected angle, which makes contributions memorable.

children.title: Participation techniques and mock GD
children.definition: Speak to the group rather than to the evaluator, build on others ideas, and practise with mock discussions.

card.explanation: A group discussion is a timed conversation among several candidates, watched for content, communication and teamwork. It assesses knowledge, reasoning, leadership, listening and whether you can work with people who disagree with you. The process runs from the introduction of the topic, through individual opinions and agreement building, to a conclusion before the time runs out. Preparation means reading widely and keeping facts ready. Enter early but politely, speak to the group rather than to the evaluator, and build on what others have said. Lateral thinking, looking at the problem from an unexpected angle, makes a contribution memorable.
card.example: On the topic of mobile phones in class, most speakers argue for or against. A lateral contribution asks what the phone is replacing, which opens a line nobody else has taken.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a group discussion?
options: To assess knowledge, reasoning, leadership and teamwork
quiz.why: Evaluators watch how you think and how you work with the group, not only what you say.

quiz.q: Which statement about group discussion is NOT correct?
options: Speak to the group rather than to the evaluator
Building on others' ideas is valued
quiz.why: Interrupting reads as poor teamwork, which is one of the things being assessed.

quiz.q: What does lateral thinking add to a discussion?
options: An unexpected angle that makes the contribution memorable
quiz.why: A fresh angle stands out when everyone else has taken the same two positions.

quiz.q: Who should you address when speaking in a group discussion?
quiz.why: Addressing the group shows you are trying to build agreement, which is the point.

quiz.q: Which is a sign of a discussion going well?
options: The group reaching a conclusion within the time limit
quiz.why: A clear conclusion before time runs out shows the group worked together.

card.examTip: Give the discussion stages, three participation techniques, and say what lateral thinking adds.

topics.title: Body Language
topics.definition: Body language is non verbal communication through posture, gestures, facial expression, eye contact and space.

children.title: Origin and development of body language
children.definition: Inherited and learned signals that developed before speech as a way to convey danger, interest and intent.

children.title: Body language as a tool for personality identification
children.definition: Habits such as posture, handshake and eye contact give clues about confidence and attitude.

children.title: Analysis of body language
children.definition: The main areas are kinesics or gestures, proxemics or space, haptics or touch, oculesics or eye contact, and paralanguage or voice.

children.title: Types of body language
children.definition: Positive and open signals versus negative and closed signals such as folded arms and avoiding eye contact.

children.title: Desirable body language
children.definition: An open posture, steady eye contact, relaxed gestures, an appropriate distance and a genuine smile.

children.title: Attitude and body language
children.definition: Attitudes shape posture and expression, and changing posture can in turn influence attitude.

children.title: Body language as powerful communication
children.definition: Consistency between words and body language builds credibility; mismatch signals deception.

card.explanation: Body language is the non verbal side of a message: posture, gestures, facial expression, eye contact and the space you keep. It developed before speech as a way to signal danger, interest and intent. Analysts divide it into areas: kinesics for gestures, proxemics for space, haptics for touch, oculesics for eye contact and paralanguage for the voice. Signals are read as open or closed, and folded arms with no eye contact reads as closed. The useful rule is consistency: when words and body agree the speaker is believed, and when they clash the body wins.
card.example: A candidate saying they are confident while staring at the floor sends two messages. The panel believes the floor, not the words.

quiz.q: Which term covers the study of personal space?
quiz.why: Proxemics is space, kinesics is gesture, haptics is touch and oculesics is eye contact.

quiz.q: Which of these is a closed body language signal?
quiz.why: Folded arms and avoiding eye contact read as defensive or closed to an observer.

quiz.q: Which statement about body language is NOT correct?
options: Body language matters less than words when the two disagree
Paralanguage covers the voice rather than the words
Posture can influence attitude as well as reflect it
quiz.why: When the two clash, people believe the body, which is why consistency builds credibility.

quiz.q: What does haptics study?
quiz.why: Haptics is communication through touch, such as a handshake or a pat on the back.

quiz.q: What is paralanguage?
options: The tone, pitch and pace of the voice rather than the words
quiz.why: How something is said often carries more meaning than the words chosen.

card.examTip: Name the five areas of body language analysis, then list four desirable signals for an interview.

topics.title: Negotiation Techniques
topics.definition: Negotiation is the process of reaching an agreement between parties with partly different interests.

children.title: Meaning and importance
children.definition: Settling prices, salaries, contracts and resources without damaging relationships.

children.title: Fundamentals of negotiation
children.definition: Interests rather than positions, the zone of possible agreement and the best alternative to a negotiated agreement.

children.title: Preparation and techniques
children.definition: Know your limits and alternatives, set objectives, decide the opening offer and consider integrative options.

children.title: Managing the process of negotiation
children.definition: Explore, signal, propose, bargain and close, with active listening throughout.

children.title: Interpersonal behaviour and case studies
children.definition: Trust, patience, emotional control and cultural sensitivity decide outcomes.

children.title: Mock negotiation
children.definition: Practice sessions that reveal how concessions and tactics affect the final agreement.

card.explanation: Negotiation reaches an agreement between parties whose interests partly differ, over prices, salaries, contracts or resources. The fundamentals are to bargain over interests rather than fixed positions, and to find the zone where a deal is possible. Know your best alternative if the talks fail. Preparation means fixing your limits, your objective and your opening offer before you sit down. The process moves through exploring, signalling, proposing, bargaining and closing, with listening throughout. Trust, patience and emotional control decide the outcome as much as the numbers do.
card.example: Two departments both want the same room. Arguing over who gets it is positional; asking what each needs the room for often reveals a timetable that suits both.

quiz.q: What does BATNA stand for?
options: Best alternative to a negotiated agreement
quiz.why: Knowing your fallback is what gives you the confidence to walk away.

quiz.q: Why negotiate over interests rather than positions?
options: Interests reveal what each side actually needs, which opens more options
quiz.why: A position is one answer, while an interest can usually be met in several ways.

quiz.q: Which statement about negotiation is NOT correct?
options: The opening offer should be your final limit
Fix your limits before you begin
quiz.why: The opening offer leaves room to move; revealing your limit at once removes it.

quiz.q: What is the zone of possible agreement?
options: The gap that cannot be closed
The room where talks are held
The overlap between what one side will accept and the other will give
quiz.why: A deal exists only where the two sides' acceptable ranges overlap.

quiz.q: Which stage comes last in the negotiation process?
quiz.why: Closing confirms the agreement, after exploring, signalling, proposing and bargaining.

card.examTip: Define the fundamentals, then list the five process stages and three personal qualities that matter.

topics.title: Meetings and Seminars
topics.definition: A meeting is a planned gathering of people to discuss and decide, and a seminar is a presentation followed by discussion.

children.title: Meaning, importance and objectives
children.definition: Meetings coordinate work, share information, solve problems and record decisions.

children.title: Leading and participating in meetings
children.definition: The chair sets the agenda and keeps time while participants prepare, contribute and listen.

children.title: Success indicators and pitfalls
children.definition: A clear decision, assigned actions and a closing summary indicate success; lack of agenda or domination by one person causes failure.

children.title: Process of meetings
children.definition: Notice, agenda, quorum, discussion, resolution, minutes and follow up.

children.title: Communication skills for meetings
children.definition: Concise speaking, note taking, constructive disagreement and summarising.

children.title: Mock meetings and seminars
children.definition: Simulated practice that builds the confidence to speak in formal settings.

card.explanation: A meeting is a planned gathering held to discuss and decide, and a seminar adds a presentation before the discussion. Meetings coordinate work, share information, solve problems and leave a written record of what was decided. The chair sets the agenda and keeps time, while participants prepare, contribute and listen. The process runs notice, agenda, quorum, discussion, resolution, minutes and follow up. A meeting succeeds when it ends with a clear decision, named owners for each action and a summary. It fails when there is no agenda or one person dominates.
card.example: A staff meeting with no agenda drifts for an hour and decides nothing. The same meeting with three listed items finishes in twenty minutes with two actions assigned.

quiz.q: What is a quorum?
options: The minimum number of members who must be present for decisions to count
The time limit of a meeting
quiz.why: Without a quorum the meeting can talk but cannot formally decide anything.

quiz.q: Which statement about meetings is NOT correct?
options: Follow up is part of the process
The agenda is written after the meeting
The chair sets the agenda and keeps time
quiz.why: The agenda goes out before the meeting so that participants can prepare.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a meeting and a seminar?
options: A seminar adds a presentation before the discussion
quiz.why: A seminar leads with a talk on a topic, then opens the floor for questions.

quiz.q: Which sign shows a meeting has succeeded?
options: It ran for a long time
It ended with named owners for each action
quiz.why: Assigned actions with names and dates are what turn discussion into results.

quiz.q: What is the usual cause of a failed meeting?
options: No agenda, or one person dominating
quiz.why: Without structure or shared airtime, the meeting produces talk rather than decisions.

card.examTip: Write the seven process steps in order, then give three success indicators and two pitfalls.

topics.title: Management Communication Relationships
topics.definition: Management communication is the flow of information that coordinates work inside an organisation.

children.title: Communication in management
children.definition: Planning, organising, leading and controlling all depend on timely and accurate communication.

children.title: Semantics and meaning
children.definition: The same word can mean different things to different people, which creates misunderstanding.

children.title: Employee and employer communication
children.definition: Grievance handling, feedback, appraisal discussion and suggestion schemes.

children.title: Downward and upward communication
children.definition: Downward carries instructions, policies and feedback; upward carries reports, suggestions and complaints.

children.title: Lateral, diagonal and informal communication
children.definition: Peer communication between departments, cross level communication and the grapevine.

children.title: Communication by specialists
children.definition: Technical and staff specialists translate expert knowledge for the rest of the organisation.

children.title: The union role in communication
children.definition: Unions represent workers in negotiations and carry collective concerns to management.

card.explanation: Management communication is the flow of information that holds an organisation together. Planning, organising, leading and controlling all depend on it arriving on time and being accurate. Downward communication carries instructions, policies and feedback to those who do the work. Upward communication carries reports, suggestions and complaints back to those who decide. Lateral communication moves between departments at the same level, diagonal cuts across levels, and the informal grapevine runs beside all of them. Specialists have a particular duty: translating expert knowledge into language everyone can act on.
card.example: An engineer explains a server fault to management in plain terms and one recommended action. That translation is what lets a decision be taken the same day.

quiz.q: Which direction carries reports, suggestions and complaints?
quiz.why: Upward communication brings what the front line knows back to the people who decide.

quiz.q: What is lateral communication?
options: Between a manager and a subordinate
Between people or departments at the same level
From the top to the bottom
quiz.why: Lateral means sideways, between peers who must coordinate without reporting to each other.

quiz.q: Which statement about management communication is NOT correct?
options: Planning and controlling depend on accurate information
The grapevine is the informal channel
Semantics means one word can mean different things to different people
Diagonal communication follows the strict chain of command
quiz.why: Diagonal communication deliberately cuts across levels and functions, unlike the formal chain.

quiz.q: Why is semantics a management concern?
options: The same word can mean different things, causing misunderstanding
quiz.why: Meaning sits in the receiver, so a word the sender finds obvious may land differently.

quiz.q: What role do unions play in organisational communication?
options: They represent workers and carry collective concerns to management
quiz.why: A union gathers individual concerns into one voice for negotiation.

card.examTip: Draw the directions of communication flow with an example of each, then add the specialist and union roles.

topics.title: Presentations
topics.definition: A presentation is a structured talk supported by visuals that informs, persuades or trains an audience.

children.title: Meaning and types of presentation
children.definition: Informative, persuasive, instructional, motivational and impromptu presentations.

children.title: Understanding the audience
children.definition: Audience size, knowledge level, expectations and attitude decide content and tone.

children.title: Planning and designing the presentation
children.definition: Define the objective, build a clear structure and choose suitable visuals for each part.

children.title: Written and oral presentation
children.definition: A written report allows detail and rereading while an oral talk allows immediate interaction.

children.title: Making use of notes and outlines
children.definition: Cue cards and a short outline keep the speaker on track without reading out a script.

children.title: Techniques for delivering presentation
children.definition: Strong opening, eye contact, voice modulation, controlled pace, purposeful gestures and a clear conclusion.

children.title: Personal style and model presentation
children.definition: Developing a natural style and studying a model presentation to improve delivery.

card.explanation: A presentation is a structured talk, usually supported by visuals, that informs, persuades or trains. Types include informative, persuasive, instructional, motivational and impromptu presentations. Everything starts with the audience: their size, knowledge, expectations and attitude decide both content and tone. Planning means fixing one objective, building a structure and choosing a visual for each part. Delivery depends on a strong opening, eye contact, voice modulation, controlled pace, purposeful gestures and a clear conclusion.
card.example: Explaining a new library system to staff is an instructional presentation. Persuading them to adopt it early is a persuasive one, and it needs a different opening.

quiz.q: Which presentation type aims to change what the audience believes or does?
quiz.why: Persuasive talks argue for a position, while informative ones only explain.

quiz.q: Why should a presentation start from the audience?
options: Because their knowledge and expectations decide the content and tone
quiz.why: A talk that assumes the wrong level loses the audience in the first minute.

quiz.q: Which statement about presentations is NOT correct?
options: Reading a full script aloud is the best delivery
One clear objective keeps the talk focused
Cue cards help the speaker stay on track
quiz.why: Reading a script loses eye contact and sounds flat, which is why outlines are preferred.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a written report over an oral presentation?
options: It allows detail and can be reread
quiz.why: A reader can go back over a table or argument, which a listener cannot.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a delivery technique listed in the syllabus?
quiz.why: Delivery is about the voice, the eyes, the pace and gesture, not about writing.

card.examTip: List the five types, then give the six delivery techniques and three planning steps.
